A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same clipping framework and convergence results. Their text, equations, plots, and complete appendices are readable. The original synthetic experiments can be matched to their relocated presentation in v2 Appendix H.

before.justification: Section 4 and Figures 1–2 report original synthetic optimization experiments, summarized over 100 runs.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix H report original regression experiments on two real datasets and retain the synthetic experiments.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 replaces projection onto an arbitrary feasible set X with projection onto B(x0,R), explicitly supplying an initial-distance bound R for adaptive variants. The five clipping and stepsize rules in Table 1, double sampling, and selective averaging remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only a synthetic quartic objective with additive Gaussian noise. v2 adds quartic-loss linear regression on California Housing and Parkinsons Telemonitoring, substantially broadening evaluation to real data. The synthetic task remains in Appendix H.

E2.justification: Both versions compare standard, implicit, and adaptive clipping, unclipped SGD and adaptive SGD, and the same sampling and averaging alternatives. v2 reuses these comparators on the added datasets. Splitting the original combined comparison into pairwise panels does not remove comparators.

E3.justification: The new regression experiments introduce preprocessing and joint tuning of learning rate and clipping threshold through a two-dimensional, two-level grid search. Their plots extend to 2000 gradient evaluations, with a separate iteration-budget comparison. The retained synthetic experiment still uses T=1000 and its original scalar stepsize-multiplier search.

E4.justification: v2 extends the single-versus-double sampling and selective-versus-all-iterate averaging ablations to both real datasets, using gradient and iteration budgets. This substantially expands evidence about the practical value of the theoretically motivated choices. The original synthetic ablations remain in Figure 6.

E5.justification: v2 specifies 10 runs for the new real-data experiments, while retaining 100 runs for the synthetic experiments. Both versions report medians and interquartile shading; the original experiments do not undergo a reported reduction in repetitions.

E6.justification: Figures 1–4 add dataset-dependent findings: clipping helps adaptive SGD on California Housing but hurts it on Parkinsons, while selective averaging slightly helps on California Housing and approximately ties ordinary averaging on Parkinsons. These are new experimental results under new settings. The original synthetic curves are retained in Figures 5–6.

T1.justification: Section 3 replaces optimization over arbitrary closed convex X with a globally defined objective on R^d. The adaptive guarantee replaces diam(X) <= R with an initial-distance bound and ball projection, substantively revising theorem and lemma assumptions while retaining the rates and most derivations. The formal setup loses its explicit unbiased-oracle condition, although proofs still use it. Lemmas 9 and 12 also retain distance bounds of R despite the revised ball projection generally guaranteeing only 2R.

C1.justification: The central high-probability convergence, adaptive-clipping, and conservative-threshold contributions remain. v2 adds the explicit novelty claim that avoiding precise knowledge of L1 was not established in the deterministic literature. Removing double sampling from the abstract does not remove that qualification from the introduction or algorithm.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of the minimizer, distance-bound, and noise assumptions and interprets the new dataset-dependent outcomes. It presents selective averaging as empirically supported on California Housing. However, Appendix H also reverses v1's synthetic interpretation, claiming Figure 6c favors Algorithm 1 even though the retained plot and legend favor averaging all iterates.

D1.justification: Appendix H adds substantial implementation documentation: missing-value handling, standardization, categorical encoding, shuffling, an intercept column, experimental stepsize formulas, method-specific tuning ranges, dataset licenses, and NVIDIA T4 hardware on Google Colab. The original synthetic setup and tuning details are retained.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through literature connecting convex optimization theory to neural-network practice and work obtaining high-probability guarantees under weaker noise assumptions. It also adds dataset references and elaborates the comparison with concurrent stochastic-convex work. The central comparison with prior generalized-smoothness convergence rates remains.

P1.justification: The introduction is extensively reorganized around convex-setting motivation and contributions. The formal setup is integrated into Section 3, assumption explanations are added, and the experimental narrative is rewritten around real-data results. Synthetic experiments and their setup move into a new experimental appendix.

P2.justification: v2 adds four figures for the real-data experiments and redisplays the original synthetic figures as Figures 5–6. Combined comparisons are split into pairwise panels, ablations become single-row three-panel displays, and legends, colors, line styles, and captions are revised.

improvement.justification: The added real-data experiments and implementation details improve empirical relevance and reproducibility, and the revised domain better supports the smoothness lemma. However, v2 introduces an interpretation contradicting its retained Figure 6c, omits the explicit unbiased-oracle assumption from the formal setup, and leaves adaptive-proof distance bounds inconsistent with the new radius definition. These unresolved issues affect both empirical interpretation and the paper's central theoretical guarantees, preventing a reliable judgment of net overall improvement.
